principles.name: Be curious to learn and grow
principles.description: Tackle the Internet's hardest problems with a drive to learn. Ask what, how and why, and challenge the status quo.
evidence_signals: Dug into how something works below what the job required, and has an artifact to show for it
Learned a new domain or tool quickly to solve a real problem
Describes feedback that changed how they work

principles.name: Communicate clearly and transparently
principles.description: Share information openly, do not hold back what others need, and be accountable in public, including for mistakes.
evidence_signals: Tells the unflattering version of a story: what broke, who was hit, and their own part
Explains a complex technical idea in plain words without jargon
Kept stakeholders informed early when a plan changed

principles.name: Do the right thing
principles.description: Act with integrity and make principled decisions, even when the easy option is tempting or the cost is real.
evidence_signals: Chose the right call over the easy one and names what it cost
Reasons about right and wrong out loud, not only about metrics
Raised a concern even though it was awkward

principles.name: Embrace diversity
principles.description: Seek out different backgrounds and points of view, and build for a global user base.
evidence_signals: Describes a different perspective that actually changed a decision
Considered users in other regions, languages or with fewer resources

principles.name: Get your work across the finish line
principles.description: Own the result end to end. Ship early, iterate, and see the work through to a real outcome.
evidence_signals: Shows how they knew the work was really done, with a measured result
Shipped a small first version and iterated on real usage
Pushed through blockers instead of handing the problem off

principles.name: Lead with empathy
principles.description: Understand customers and colleagues and act with care for them.
evidence_signals: Names a specific customer or teammate and what they needed
Handled a disagreement while respecting the other person's view
Helped or mentored someone with a visible result

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background, motivation, why Cloudflare, and logistics. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager screen
rounds.notes: Often early in the process. Resume, past projects, interest in the team, and the reasons behind past architecture choices.

rounds.name: Technical phone screen
rounds.notes: Live coding, usually one medium problem or a practical task such as a rate limiter or log parser. Some teams use a take-home instead. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Coding and debugging
rounds.notes: Practical coding or finding a defect in unfamiliar code. Some loops allow an AI coding assistant. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: System design
rounds.notes: Distributed systems at the edge: global key-value store, rate limiter in a proxy, log collection from data centers. Often without managed cloud services. Follow-ups on 100x traffic and data center failure. Networking basics (DNS, TLS, anycast) may come up.

rounds.name: Orange Cloud interview
rounds.notes: Values round on the Cloudflare Capabilities: mistakes, disagreements, learning, and motivation. Short and tightly timed.

rounds.name: Executive call
rounds.notes: Vision, values and long-term goals. Reported to happen for most candidates.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: PM background and interest in Cloudflare. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager interview
rounds.notes: Deep dive into product experience, process and strategic thinking. Technical depth and B2B or security experience help.

rounds.name: Take-home case and panel presentation
rounds.interviewer_role: Panel of product managers and engineers
rounds.notes: A product case or strategy exercise done at home, then presented and defended in front of a panel.

rounds.name: Cross-functional interviews
rounds.interviewer_role: Engineering manager, designer or peer PM
rounds.notes: Working with engineering, scoping, and handling conflicting requests.

rounds.name: Orange Cloud interview
rounds.notes: Values round on the Cloudflare Capabilities.

rounds.name: Executive interview
rounds.notes: Vision and fit.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Solutions engineering (pre-sales). Motivation, background and what the candidate knows about Cloudflare. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager screen
rounds.notes: Sales engineering experience, customer-facing skills and technical depth.

rounds.name: Technical interview
rounds.notes: Rapid networking and security questions: DNS, TLS, BGP, HTTP, proxies, latency, DDoS, WAF and Zero Trust.

rounds.name: Take-home setup task
rounds.notes: Hands-on setup such as putting a domain behind Cloudflare and enforcing HTTPS, over about a week. Duration is a placeholder. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Panel demo
rounds.interviewer_role: Panel of sales, customer success, support and solutions engineers
rounds.notes: Present a Cloudflare product or customer case and handle questions as if from a customer. Tie features to customer outcomes.

rounds.name: Orange Cloud interview
rounds.notes: Values round on the Cloudflare Capabilities.

rounds.name: Director and executive calls
rounds.interviewer_role: Head of solutions engineering or a VP
rounds.notes: Situational fit and motivation.

question_patterns.pattern: A mistake that hurt production or customers, told honestly: what broke, own part, the response, and what stops it from happening again
A disagreement with a peer or manager about a technical or product decision, how it was raised, and how it ended
Something the candidate investigated deeply because it bothered them, and what they found
values: Be curious to learn and grow

question_patterns.pattern: A choice between the convenient option and the principled one, and the cost of choosing
Explain a complex technical concept to a non-technical person, often live in the interview
A decision made or a project finished with incomplete information or unclear requirements, and how the result was confirmed
values: Get your work across the finish line

question_patterns.pattern: Motivation for Cloudflare and the team, including which Cloudflare products the candidate has used
values: Be curious to learn and grow

question_patterns.pattern: Walk through a past project and the reasons behind its main architecture or product choices
values: Get your work across the finish line

question_patterns.pattern: Design a globally distributed service that runs across many data centers, then handle much more traffic and a data center failure
Explain how a core Internet protocol or request path works, step by step, at the depth the role needs
values: Be curious to learn and grow

question_patterns.pattern: Diagnose a failing request or service: state a hypothesis, test it, and narrow the cause
Prioritize features or design a product for a security or performance product, for a named customer segment, with success metrics
Present a Cloudflare solution to a customer with a specific problem and handle their technical and business objections

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a mistake you made that affected production. What happened and how did you handle it?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Give the honest version first: what broke, who was affected, for how long, and the candidate's own part without softening it. Then the response: how it was detected, who was told and when, and how it was fixed. Close with the lasting change (a test, alert, rollout step or runbook) and what the candidate does differently now. The tone should match a good public post-mortem: factual, no blame on others. Pitfalls: a trivial mistake, hiding the candidate's role, or no prevention step.

looking_for: Whether you tell the honest version of a mistake
How you respond and stop it from happening again
strong_signals: States your own part plainly
Names the lasting fix, such as a test or alert
watch_outs: Blaming others or no prevention step

sample_questions.question: Describe a time you disagreed with a technical decision. What did you do?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Set out the decision, the candidate's concern, and why the concern was credible, with data. Show how they raised it: directly, to the right person, early enough to matter. Show that they listened to the other side and say what they learned from it. Give the outcome either way: they changed the decision, or they committed to it and helped it work. Pitfalls: a story where the candidate was simply right and others were wrong, or going quiet and complaining later.

looking_for: How you raise a concern and back it with evidence
Whether you listen to the other side
strong_signals: Raises the issue early with data
Commits and helps once the decision is made
watch_outs: You were right and everyone else was wrong
Complaining later instead of speaking up

sample_questions.question: Explain a complex technical concept you know well to someone with no technical background.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick one concept the candidate knows deeply, such as DNS or caching. Start with why it matters to the listener, then use one simple analogy and build up in two or three steps. Avoid jargon or define it at once. Check understanding and adjust. Keep it to about two minutes. Pitfalls: a lecture full of acronyms, an analogy that breaks on the first follow-up, or picking a topic the candidate cannot go deeper on.

looking_for: Whether you can make a hard idea simple
Whether you adjust to the listener
strong_signals: Starts with why it matters to the listener
One clear analogy, about two minutes
watch_outs: An analogy that breaks on the first follow-up

sample_questions.question: Why Cloudflare? Which of our products have you actually used?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Connect to the mission of helping build a better Internet with a specific, personal reason. Name Cloudflare products the candidate has really used, even on the free plan (DNS, Workers, Tunnel, Pages), what they built, and what they liked or would change. Tie this to the team and role. Strong answers show the candidate has looked under the hood. Pitfalls: generic praise, only reading the website, or naming products they cannot discuss.
values: Be curious to learn and grow

looking_for: Real interest in the mission and products
Whether you have tried the products yourself
strong_signals: Names a product you used and what you built
Says what you would change

sample_questions.question: Tell me about something you investigated deeply just because it bothered you.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe a real puzzle, such as odd latency, a strange protocol behavior or a flaky test, and why the candidate could not let it go. Walk through how they dug in: tools, experiments, what they read. Share what they found and any artifact (a write-up, a fix, a side project). Close with what it taught them and how it helped the team. Pitfalls: claiming curiosity without evidence, or a story that ends without a finding.
values: Be curious to learn and grow

looking_for: Real curiosity about how things work
How you investigate a puzzle
strong_signals: Shows the tools and experiments you used
Has an artifact such as a write-up or fix

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to choose between the easy call and the right call.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Lay out both options and what made the easy one tempting (deadline, pressure, a metric). Explain why the candidate saw the other option as right, reasoning out loud about users, trust or integrity, not only numbers. Show what the choice cost and how they got others on board. Give the outcome and whether they would choose the same again. Pitfalls: an option that cost nothing, or a choice that was really just a preference.

looking_for: Whether you act on principle under pressure
How you reason about right and wrong
strong_signals: Names the real cost of the right call
Explains how you brought others along

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a decision you had to make with incomplete information.
sample_questions.strong_answer: State what was unknown and why waiting was not an option. Show how the candidate reduced the risk: what they checked quickly, which assumptions they wrote down, and whether the decision was easy to reverse. Explain how they told others about the uncertainty. Give the result and what they learned when the missing facts arrived. Pitfalls: a decision with no real uncertainty, or no plan for being wrong.
values: Get your work across the finish line

looking_for: How you act when facts are missing
How you manage the risk of being wrong
strong_signals: Writes down assumptions and checks them
Tells others about the uncertainty
watch_outs: No real uncertainty in the story

sample_questions.question: Design a rate limiting service that runs inside an HTTP proxy deployed in data centers around the world.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify limits (per IP, per API key, per path), accuracy needs and latency budget. Pick an algorithm (token bucket or sliding window) and explain why. Discuss where counters live: local per server, shared per data center, or synced globally, and the accuracy versus latency trade-off. Cover hot keys, memory limits, clock skew, and failing open or closed when the store is down. Explain behavior at 100x traffic. Pitfalls: a single central counter for the whole world, or ignoring failure modes.

looking_for: How you choose and justify a limiting algorithm
Where counters live and why
strong_signals: Weighs accuracy against latency across data centers
Decides fail open or closed and explains it
watch_outs: One central counter for the whole world

sample_questions.question: Design a system that collects logs from servers in hundreds of data centers and makes them searchable, without managed cloud services.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify volume, retention, query patterns and how fresh data must be. Cover collection on each server, buffering and batching, transport over unreliable links, and a queue such as Kafka before storage. Choose a store for fast queries (for example a column store such as ClickHouse) and explain partitioning by time and customer. Handle back pressure, data center outages, duplicates and sampling at peak load. Pitfalls: assuming a managed service does the hard parts, or ignoring cost of storage.

looking_for: How you move data reliably across a global network
How you pick storage for the query patterns
strong_signals: Handles back pressure and data center outages
Partitions by time and customer
watch_outs: Relying on a managed service for the hard parts

sample_questions.question: Design a globally distributed key-value store for configuration that must reach every data center quickly.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify read and write rates, value size, and how fast and how consistent updates must be. Explain a central source of truth with replication out to the edge, versus fully distributed writes, and the consistency model each gives. Cover caching at the edge, versioning, rollbacks of bad config, partial outages and network partitions. Strong answers connect the design to safety: a bad config pushed everywhere at once is a global outage, so discuss staged rollout. Pitfalls: claiming strong consistency and low latency everywhere for free.

looking_for: Your consistency model and why
How updates reach the edge safely
strong_signals: Discusses staged rollout and rollback of bad data
Handles partitions and partial outages
watch_outs: Strong consistency and low latency for free
No plan for a bad config push

sample_questions.question: Walk me through what happens when a user types a web address into a browser and presses Enter.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Go in order: DNS resolution (cache, resolver, root, TLD, authoritative), TCP or QUIC connection, the TLS handshake and certificate check, the HTTP request, and the response. Add where a proxy or CDN sits: anycast routing to a nearby data center, cache hit or miss, and a request to the origin. Mention where it can fail or be slow. Go deeper where the interviewer asks. Pitfalls: skipping TLS or DNS steps, or naming terms without explaining what they do.
values: Be curious to learn and grow

looking_for: Accurate knowledge of the request path
Where a CDN or proxy fits in
strong_signals: Covers DNS, connection, TLS and HTTP in order
Explains anycast and cache hit or miss

sample_questions.question: Can a request from London to Sydney ever take under 5 milliseconds? Explain.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Estimate the distance (about 17,000 km) and the speed of light in fiber (about 200,000 km per second). One way takes about 85 ms, so a round trip is well over 150 ms. Under 5 ms is impossible for a real round trip. Then explain how it can look possible: the request is answered by a nearby data center through anycast and caching, so the user in London never reaches Sydney. Pitfalls: guessing without numbers, or missing the edge caching point.

looking_for: Whether you reason from physics with rough numbers
Whether you see how the edge changes the answer
strong_signals: Estimates distance and speed of light in fiber
Explains answering from a nearby data center

sample_questions.question: A user gets a 500 error from a site behind a proxy. How would you find the cause?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start by scoping: one user or all, one path or all, since when, and what changed. Separate whether the error comes from the proxy or the origin, using response headers and logs. Check the origin directly, then recent deploys, config, certificates and resource limits. State a hypothesis, test it, and narrow down. Explain what to tell the customer while it is open. Pitfalls: jumping to a fix without evidence, or not checking what changed.

looking_for: A systematic way to narrow down a failure
Whether you split proxy from origin
strong_signals: Scopes the problem and asks what changed
States and tests a hypothesis
watch_outs: Jumping to a fix without evidence

sample_questions.question: A customer is under repeated DDoS attacks. Walk me through the solution you would propose.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Ask discovery questions first: what is attacked (website, API, network), attack size and type, current setup, and business impact. Propose a layered answer: network-level protection, proxying the web layer, WAF and rate limiting, bot management, and hiding the origin. Explain onboarding steps and risks such as DNS changes. Tie each part to the customer's outcome (uptime, cost, staff time) and state how success is measured. Pitfalls: listing products without discovery, or ignoring latency and onboarding concerns.

looking_for: Whether you ask discovery questions first
How you link the solution to business outcomes
strong_signals: Proposes layered protection by attack type
Covers onboarding steps and risks

sample_questions.question: How would you explain Zero Trust security to a non-technical executive who must approve the budget?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start from the executive's concern: breaches, remote work, cost of VPNs. Explain the idea in one sentence: every request is checked for who and what, not trusted because it is inside the network. Use a simple analogy, give one concrete example from their business, and end with the outcome, risk reduced and a rough path to roll out. Invite questions. Pitfalls: acronyms, a feature list, or no link to business risk.

looking_for: Whether you speak to the executive's concerns
Whether you make the idea simple and concrete
strong_signals: One-sentence idea plus one business example
Ends with risk reduced and a rollout path

sample_questions.question: How would you prioritize features for a web application firewall product?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick the customer segment first (self-serve small sites or large enterprises) and their top pains, such as false positives, setup effort or new attack types. List candidate features and judge each by customer impact, reach, effort, and fit with the platform. Use data a network operator trusts: blocked attacks, false positive rate, time to set up. Make a clear call, say what is cut and why, and define success metrics. Pitfalls: no segment, a framework with no decision, or ignoring the free plan.

looking_for: Whether you start from a customer segment
How you make and defend a clear call
strong_signals: Uses metrics such as false positive rate
Says what is cut and why

sample_questions.question: Design a new product that helps small businesses protect themselves from bots.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define the user: a small business owner with little security knowledge and a tight budget. Name the bot problems that hurt them most (fake sign-ups, scraping, card testing) and pick one to focus on. Propose a simple, mostly automatic solution with safe defaults, and say what is free and what is paid. Cover how to avoid blocking real customers. Define success metrics such as bad traffic blocked and false positives, and a first small launch. Pitfalls: an enterprise-style product with many settings, or no focus.
values: Get your work across the finish line

looking_for: Whether you understand the small business user
How you focus on one problem
strong_signals: Safe defaults with little setup
Clear metrics including false positives
watch_outs: Many settings a small owner cannot use
Trying to solve every bot problem at once

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time sales and engineering wanted different things from your product. How did you handle it?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe both requests and what was behind each: a deal at risk, or technical debt and capacity. Show how the candidate got the facts (customer demand, revenue, effort, risk) and brought both sides together. Explain the decision, how it was communicated, and what each side gave up. Close with the result and what the candidate changed in their process. Pitfalls: siding with whoever is louder, or a compromise that pleased no one.

looking_for: How you balance competing internal requests
Whether you decide with facts
strong_signals: Understands what is behind each request
Explains the decision openly to both sides
watch_outs: A compromise that pleased no one

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Embedded in a team with a mentor; ships a concrete deliverable that solves a real customer or internal problem.
Builds and ships features within a team, writes production code with good error handling, and explains design choices.
Owns systems and their architecture, handles failure at global scale, and guides other engineers.
Sets long-term technical direction for critical systems, leads architecture across teams, and mentors engineers. Postings ask for about 8 to 10 or more years.
Owns features in a technical B2B product, works closely with engineering, and decides with data.
Owns a product area, its strategy and metrics, and influences without authority across engineering, sales and support.
Runs technical discovery, demos and proofs of concept for customers, with strong networking and security basics.
Leads technical work on large or complex accounts, designs customer architectures, and feeds customer needs back to product.

persona.tone: Friendly, curious and direct; values plain honesty over polish
persona.pace: Brisk; the values round is short and tightly timed, so answers should be about 90 seconds to two minutes
persona.pushback_style: Asks 'what did you personally do?', 'what broke and what did you change?', and in technical rounds 'what happens at 100 times the traffic or when a data center fails?'; flags rehearsed-sounding answers
persona.closing_style: Leaves a few minutes for the candidate's questions and expects curious questions about the product or team

case_style.notes: PM cases are technical B2B: prioritizing or designing security, performance or developer products for a named customer segment, with metrics a network operator trusts. Solutions engineer cases are customer pitches and demos. Market sizing is rarely reported.

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: the six Capabilities and the three values (Principled, Curious, Transparent) come from the official careers page; descriptions are our paraphrase, and principle weights are our estimate.

loop_structure: the official page gives only the stages (recruiter, team panel, executive calls with the Orange Cloud interview); round names, durations and interviewer roles come from prep sites and candidate reports that vary by team and region. The solutions engineer take-home duration is a placeholder.

bar_by_level: Cloudflare does not publish a level ladder. Levels.fyi shows crowdsourced L1 to L5 codes with no public title mapping, so we use public job titles (Systems Engineer, Senior, Principal; Product Manager, Senior PM; Solutions Engineer, Senior). Scope text is our summary from job postings and the intern blog post.
persona: inferred from prep-site advice (short timed values round, rehearsed answers flagged, follow-ups on scale and failure); there is no official description of interviewer style.
scoring_weights: estimated from the Capabilities and prep-site evaluation criteria; no public source gives weights.
case_style: based on a small number of reported PM and solutions engineer questions from CleverPrep; PM loops are reported inconsistently (four to six rounds, with or without a take-home).
sample_questions: PM and solutions engineer questions come from CleverPrep and Nora, prep sites that aggregate candidate reports; system design questions come from TechPrep.
